questions.question: How do you read a Java stack trace to find the source of an error?
questions.title: How to Read a Java Stack Trace
questions.direct_answer: Read the first line for the exception type and message, then scan the 'at' lines top-to-bottom to find the first line pointing to your own code — that is usually where the bug is.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can independently diagnose errors without hand-holding
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Reading stack traces top-down through all framework lines instead of jumping to your own code
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the structure: exception → caused-by chain → identifying user code vs framework code

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A stack trace has a clear structure once you know how to read it. The very first line tells you the exception class and the message. Then there are a series of 'at' lines, each representing a method call in the call stack. The top of the stack is where the exception actually occurred. In practice, I scroll down to find the first 'at' line that refers to my own package — for example, 'at com.myapp.service.UserService.getUser(UserService.java:42)'. That line number and class name tell me exactly where to look. If there is a 'Caused by:' section, I read that too — it shows the original exception that triggered the outer one, and the root cause is usually at the bottom of the chain.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Line 1: exception class + message — what went wrong
'at' lines: call stack from most recent call at top
Find the first 'at' line in your own package — that's your bug location
'Caused by:' chains: read the innermost one for the root cause
File:line number in parentheses tells you exactly where to look

questions.question: What does 'Caused by' in a Java stack trace mean and how do you use it?
questions.title: Caused By — Nested Exceptions in Java Stack Traces
questions.direct_answer: 'Caused by' shows the original exception that triggered a wrapper exception — you should always read the innermost 'Caused by' first because it contains the true root cause.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to navigate real-world stack traces which almost always have nested exceptions
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only reading the top-level exception and missing the real cause buried in a Caused-by
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain exception chaining with initCause() — shows deeper understanding

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: In Java, you can wrap one exception inside another using exception chaining. The 'Caused by:' line in a stack trace shows the original exception that was caught before the outer one was thrown. For example, you might see 'RuntimeException: Failed to load user' at the top, and then 'Caused by: SQLException: Connection refused' below. The RuntimeException is what propagated to your code, but the real problem is the database connection failure. When I see multiple Caused-by sections, I always jump to the last one in the chain — that is the original exception, the root cause. Everything above it is just layers of wrapping.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Caused by = original exception wrapped inside a higher-level one
Frameworks commonly wrap low-level exceptions in runtime exceptions
Always read the innermost Caused-by — that's the root cause
Multiple Caused-by chains: go to the bottom of the chain first
Fix typically lives near the innermost exception, not the outer one

questions.question: How do you read a NullPointerException stack trace in Java?
questions.title: Reading a NullPointerException Stack Trace
questions.direct_answer: Find the 'at' line pointing to your code, note the line number, go to that line, and identify which object on that line could be null — Java 14+ even tells you the exact variable.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical debugging ability — NullPointerException is the most common Java exception
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Randomly adding null checks everywhere instead of pinpointing which reference is null
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Java 14 Helpful NullPointerExceptions that name the exact null variable

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: NullPointerException is probably the exception I've seen most often. When I get one, the first thing I do is find the line in my code that's in the stack trace. Say it points to UserService.java line 42. I go there and look at that line. If it's something like 'user.getAddress().getCity()', there are two possible null references: user itself, or the Address object returned by getAddress(). I need to figure out which one is null. If I'm on Java 14 or later, the exception message is more helpful — it actually says something like 'Cannot invoke getCity() because the return value of getAddress() is null', which tells me exactly which part of the chain is null.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Find the first 'at' line in your code — go to that exact line
Identify every object reference on that line that could be null
Java 14+ Helpful NPE messages name the exact null variable
Trace backward: where was this reference set? Could that return null?
Decide: is null a bug upstream, or a valid case requiring a null check here?

questions.question: How do you identify your own code versus framework code in a Java stack trace?
questions.title: Identifying Your Code vs Framework Code in a Stack Trace
questions.direct_answer: Your code appears under your package name in the 'at' lines; everything else is framework or library code — focus on your package lines first because that's where your bug lives.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical skill — candidates who can't filter framework noise waste time in wrong places
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Trying to understand every Spring/Hibernate line in a stack trace instead of jumping to application code
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention IntelliJ's 'Hide framework stacks' feature that collapses library frames

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: When I look at a stack trace from a Spring Boot application, I might see 30 or 40 lines. Most of them are Spring internals, Tomcat servlet handling, reflection calls — none of which I wrote. The key is filtering to my own package. If my application package is 'com.myapp', I quickly scan through the 'at' lines looking for anything starting with that prefix. Everything with 'org.springframework', 'java.lang.reflect', 'org.apache' — I generally skip. IntelliJ IDEA has a nice feature where it collapses framework stack frames automatically and shows your code lines highlighted. In practice, there might only be two or three lines from my own code in a 50-line stack trace, and one of those three is almost always where the bug is.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Your code: lines starting with your base package (e.g., com.mycompany.myapp)
Framework code: org.springframework, java., sun., org.hibernate — generally skip
Focus on your package lines first — your bug is almost always there
IntelliJ collapses framework frames automatically to reduce noise
Only dig into framework code when you suspect misconfiguration

questions.question: What does a StackOverflowError stack trace look like and what causes it?
questions.title: StackOverflowError — What It Looks Like and Why It Happens
questions.direct_answer: StackOverflowError occurs when infinite recursion fills the call stack; its trace shows the same method repeated hundreds of times, and the fix is to add a base case to the recursion.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of call stack mechanics and recursion
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that it's an Error not an Exception, and generally should not be caught

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: StackOverflowError has one of the most distinctive stack traces you'll ever see — the same method name repeated hundreds of times in the 'at' lines. That immediately tells me there's infinite recursion happening. Each method call adds a frame to the call stack, and when that stack exceeds its maximum size — typically a few thousand frames — Java throws StackOverflowError. The usual cause is a recursive method that's missing a base case. The fix is to identify the recursive method from the repeated lines, then find where the base case is missing or incorrect. StackOverflowError is an Error, not an Exception — you should not catch and suppress it, you should fix the recursion.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Signature: same method repeated hundreds of times in the trace
Cause: infinite recursion — base case is missing or unreachable
Each method call = one stack frame; JVM stack has a size limit
Fix: add or correct the base case in the recursive method
It's an Error not an Exception — don't catch and suppress it, fix it

questions.question: What is a chained exception (exception cause) in a Java stack trace?
questions.title: Chained Exceptions in Stack Traces
questions.direct_answer: A chained exception shows the original cause of an exception when one exception is wrapped inside another, indicated by 'Caused by:' in the stack trace.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to read complex stack traces with multiple exception layers
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only reading the first exception and missing the root cause in the 'Caused by:' section
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that the root cause is almost always at the bottom of the Caused by chain

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
A chained exception, also called exception wrapping, occurs when one exception is caught and then re-thrown wrapped inside another exception. In the stack trace, this appears as 'Caused by:' sections below the primary exception.

This is extremely common in Java applications. A typical scenario: a database driver throws a low-level SQLException, your data access code catches it and wraps it in a custom DataAccessException, and your service layer might catch that and wrap it in a ServiceException. Each layer adds context but preserves the original cause.

In the stack trace, it looks like this:
```
com.myapp.ServiceException: Failed to load user profile
    at com.myapp.UserService.loadProfile(UserService.java:45)
    ...
Caused by: com.myapp.DataAccessException: User query failed
    at com.myapp.UserRepository.findById(UserRepository.java:28)
    ...
Caused by: java.sql.SQLException: Connection refused
    at com.mysql.jdbc.Driver...
```

The most important rule when reading chained stack traces: always scroll to the bottom 'Caused by:' entry first. That's the root cause — the original thing that went wrong. In this example, the actual problem is a refused database connection. The ServiceException and DataAccessException are just layers that wrapped it.

New developers often get confused and spend time investigating the first exception in the stack trace when the real problem is buried in the last 'Caused by:'. In a Spring application particularly, you'll often see several layers of framework exceptions wrapping your actual application exception — always look at the bottom.

You create chained exceptions in your code by passing the original exception to the new exception's constructor: `throw new ServiceException('Failed', originalException);`

sections.title: Key Points
content: Chained exceptions appear as 'Caused by:' sections below the primary exception
Always read the bottom 'Caused by:' first — that's the root cause
Exception wrapping preserves the original cause while adding contextual layers
Create chained exceptions by passing the original exception to the constructor: new MyException(message, cause)

questions.question: What does 'at' mean in a Java stack trace and how do you use it to find the bug?
questions.title: Reading the 'at' Lines in Stack Traces
questions.direct_answer: Each 'at' line in a stack trace represents one method call in the call chain, showing the fully qualified class name, method, source file, and line number where execution was at the time of the exception.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical ability to navigate a stack trace and find the relevant code
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Being overwhelmed by long stack traces with framework code and not knowing which line to look at first
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the strategy of looking for your own application package lines, skipping framework internals

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Each line starting with 'at' in a stack trace represents one frame in the call stack — one method that was executing at the time the exception was thrown. Reading these correctly is the core skill for interpreting stack traces.

The format is: `at package.ClassName.methodName(FileName.java:lineNumber)`

For example:
```
at com.myapp.service.OrderService.processOrder(OrderService.java:87)
at com.myapp.controller.OrderController.createOrder(OrderController.java:42)
```

The first 'at' line (topmost) is where the exception was actually thrown. The lines below it show how the program got there — each one is the method that called the one above it. So reading top-to-bottom gives you the chain from the throw site back to the entry point.

In real Spring Boot applications, stack traces can be 50-100 lines long because they include many framework internal calls from Spring, Tomcat, and the JDK. The practical strategy is to look for lines that contain your own application's package name — usually something like `com.yourcompany.yourapp`. Those are the lines in your code that you can actually examine and fix.

A good approach:
1. Read the exception type and message first to understand what went wrong
2. Find the topmost 'at' line in your package — that's the first place in your code where the problem manifested
3. Open that file and navigate to that exact line number
4. If the cause isn't obvious there, look at the 'at' line below it in your package — that's the method that called into the failing code

IntelliJ IDEA makes this easier by making the 'at' lines clickable in the console — clicking jumps directly to that line in your source code.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Each 'at' line shows: class, method, file, and line number for one frame in the call chain
Topmost 'at' line is where the exception was thrown; subsequent lines show how you got there
In long stack traces, focus on lines matching your application's package — skip framework internals
IntelliJ makes 'at' lines clickable in the console, jumping directly to the source line

followup_questions: What does it mean if all the 'at' lines in a stack trace are in framework or JDK code?
How would you read a stack trace for a NullPointerException?

questions.question: What is a StackOverflowError and what typically causes it?
questions.title: StackOverflowError Causes
questions.direct_answer: StackOverflowError occurs when the call stack exceeds its maximum depth, most commonly caused by infinite or excessively deep recursion.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of JVM memory and recursion
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing StackOverflowError with OutOfMemoryError or not knowing what the call stack is
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain what the call stack is and how each method call adds a frame to it

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
A StackOverflowError in Java occurs when the call stack — the memory structure that tracks active method calls — runs out of space. Every time you call a method, Java pushes a new frame onto the call stack containing the method's local variables, parameters, and return address. When that method returns, its frame is popped off. The stack has a finite size, and if method calls nest too deeply, it overflows.

The most common cause is unintentional infinite recursion — a method calling itself without a proper base case that stops the recursion. For example:
```java
public int factorial(int n) {
    return n * factorial(n - 1);  // Missing base case: if (n == 0) return 1;
}
```
This will call itself indefinitely, adding a new frame to the stack on each call until the stack is full.

Another common cause is mutual recursion — method A calls method B which calls method A again, cycling indefinitely without a termination condition.

In a stack trace, StackOverflowError looks distinctive — you'll see the same one or two method names repeated hundreds or thousands of times, which is an immediate visual indicator of infinite recursion.

To fix it, you need to identify the recursion and add or correct the base case. If you legitimately need deep recursion (like traversing very deep tree structures), you might need to convert the recursive algorithm to an iterative one using an explicit stack data structure.

Note: StackOverflowError is an Error, not an Exception — it's part of the `java.lang.Error` hierarchy, meaning it signals a JVM-level condition rather than a recoverable application error.

sections.title: Key Points
content: StackOverflowError occurs when recursive method calls exhaust the call stack's fixed memory
Most common cause: missing or incorrect base case in a recursive method
In stack traces, it appears as the same method name repeated hundreds of times
Fix by adding a correct base case, or convert deep recursion to an iterative algorithm
